gloss: i.e. there will be no more of this friendly conversation in the rest of the poem. In book XI. the Messenger sent from Heaven is not Raphael “the affable Archangel,” but the stern, warlike Michael, who has to announce to Adam and Eve their banishment from Eden and to lead them forth.
much of, a deal of. Addison quotes this line to illustrate his remark that M. “often affects a kind of jingle in his words.”
inseparable companion. *Misery*, all kinds of physical pain and disease — the “harbingers,” i.e. forerunners, of death.

He means that as regards the “argument,” i.e. subject, with which it is now about to deal, his poem has an advantage over the three great classical epics: the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey*, and the *Aeneid*, which tells of the hostility of Juno to Aeneas, the son of Cytherea, i.e. Venus, and of his betrothal to Lavinia.

i.e. the “Heavenly Muse” (Urania) whose aid he invokes at the beginning of the poem. Milton’s references to this Muse of Sacred Song which gave him inspiration have a reality that is lacking in the conventional poetical appeals to the ‘Muses.’
i.e. about 1640; some lines of *Paradise Lost* (IV. 32–41) were written as early as 1642.

a mythical subject would not appeal to M. Probably one of his reasons for abandoning the story of King Arthur, which he at one time intended to take as the subject of his great poem, was that he found the story to be “fabled” and “feigned.”
all the equipments of a tournament. The allusion is to the Italian poets — e.g. Boiardo, Ariosto and Tasso — and Spenser, who describe tournaments and scenes of chivalry.

i.e. in the world’s history; implying that the conditions favourable to epic poetry had passed away. In his *Life of Milton* Johnson says: “There prevailed in his time an opinion that the world was in its decay.”

here he touches on what was a lifelong opinion. Thus in his poem *Mansus* (1638) he apologises for his Latin poems on the ground that his Muse was reared in the chill north. *years*; perhaps not far short of sixty.
cf. Job i. 7, “From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.”
cf. IV. 549–88, where Uriel is described as coming to warn Gabriel, who guarded the eastern gate of Paradise with Cherubim, that one of the outcast evil angels has found his way into the “garden.”

“Of the seven days during which Satan went round and round the Earth, three were spent in moving from east to west on the equatorial line; four in moving round from pole to pole, in which second way of moving he would traverse the two colures, viz. two great circles drawn from the poles” (Masson).
he identifies the Tigris with the river that “went out of Eden to water the garden,” Genesis ii. 10.

“The Fiend, on leaving Eden, had gone northward over the Pontus Euxinus or Black Sea, and over the Palus Maeotis or Sea of Azof, as far as beyond the Siberian river Ob. In length his journeys had extended from the Syrian river Orontes, west of Eden, to the Isthmus of Darien” (Masson).
“Now the Serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made,” Genesis iii. 1.
i.e. a debate that for a long time came to no decision in regard to the thoughts pondered over. *sentence*, decision, Lat. *sententia*.
M. is fond of comparing the motions of the stellar bodies (= “other heavens”) to a “dance.”

cf. VIII. 15–38, where dealing with the same thought M. makes Adam use the same cautious language. Probably his reason was that he thought that some of the heavenly bodies, especially the Moon, might be inhabited.
“The three kinds of life rising as it were by steps, the vegetable, animal and rational; of all which Man partakes, and he only” (Richardson).

the sense Milton intended is, no doubt: ‘I find none of these delightful places, or parts of the earth, permitted to be a residence for me; neither can I possibly escape from that hell to which I am doomed’ — the hell, namely, of his outcast condition and “torment” within him (Dunster).
meant as a sneer at the time which the work of creation had taken its Creator.
which he denies when addressing his followers, telling them that they are “self-begot, self-raised.” Yet he knew and elsewhere admitted to himself the truth.

i.e. the substance variously described as “ethereal” and “empyreal” of which M. conceived the Angelic forms to consist. That the forms of the fallen Angels changed was a doctrine taught by many of the Church Fathers.
modelled on Hebraic phrases like “sons of valour,” 2 Samuel ii. 7 (margin), “sons of Belial,” 1 Samuel ii. 12.
the simile is used again, XII. 629–31. It is Homeric (*Iliad* I. 359). The external world had been “like a mist” to the poet himself.

Newton aptly notes that M. himself was an early riser. Aubrey in his brief *Life of Milton* says that it was his custom to rise at 4.30 a.m., and that he always began the day by having the Hebrew Bible read to him.

Milton brought up his daughters on this principle. Apparently he had good reason to be satisfied in this respect with his third wife, “a genteel person,” says Aubrey, “of a peaceful and agreeable humour.”
i.e. the highest object, since “without love no happiness,” as Raphael tells Adam (VIII. 621).
Raphael, whose last words to Adam were a warning to “beware” and “stand fast” in his obedience.
in the literal sense of Lat. *integer* (from which *entire* is derived), ‘untouched by, free from.’
brow, forehead (Lat. *frons*); used with quibbling allusion to “affronts” in 328.

emphatic. The sentiment is that of the fine passage in the *Areopagitica* where M. says, “I cannot praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue,” i.e. one that does not go out into the world and face evil.
i.e. “no place of happiness, not what its name denotes,” i.e. ‘pleasure’ (Keightley).
on this point, as might be expected, M. dwells often. There is much bearing on the subject in chapters 3 and 4 — on “The divine Decrees” and “Predestination” — of *The Christian Doctrine*, I.

The rapid, rather abrupt style is meant, apparently, to indicate some displeasure on the part of Adam. Newton thought that Milton here had in mind the incident of his own wife’s leaving him soon after their marriage.
i.e. for all her submissiveness she has the last word. It is in these side-touches that M. shows his own estimate of women.

a nymph of the mountain. *Dryad*, a nymph of the wood — literally of the trees. *Delia*, Artemis or Diana, who was born in the island of Delos; the goddess of the chase, in which capacity she was attended by a “train” of nymphs.

a Roman divinity of flocks and shepherds. *Pomona*, the goddess of fruit (Lat. *pomum*). The story of Pomona’s being wooed by Vertumnus, one of the lesser rustic deities of Roman mythology, is told by Ovid in the *Metamorphoses* XIV. 623 et seq.
the goddess of agriculture, *yet virgin of*, i.e. before she had become the mother of Proserpine by Jupiter.
no doubt, M. knew, and perhaps wished to brush aside, the Rabbinical gloss that Satan assumed a form half angelical (or human), half serpentine, when he appeared to Eve.

i.e. after he was slain by the boar. According to the myth, the prayers of Aphrodite (Venus) moved the gods of the lower world to allow Adonis to return to the earth every year and pass six months with the goddess.

M. inserts these words as the allusion is to Scripture — not as before, to classical legend. *the sapient king*; referring to the Garden of Solomon mentioned in the Song of Solomon vi. 2. By “fair Egyptian spouse” M. means “Pharaoh’s daughter” (1 Kings iii. 1).

Perhaps “only a narrative of what befell the poet in his younger days, when living in his father’s house in Bread Street, in the City” (Keightley). His favourite season was spring. “He always had a garden where he lived,” says Aubrey.
i.e. “formed of earth” (149), a “man of clay” (176). *mould* = ‘material, substance’; as often in M.
Todd aptly quotes the description of Pyrrhus in the Player’s speech in *Hamlet*, “with eyes like carbuncles,” i.e. deep red (a sign of passionate temperament and anger).

lemma: not those that in Illyria changed
gloss: i.e. not those serpents that changed into themselves Hermione and Cadmus. The story how Cadmus king of Thebes and his wife Harmonia came to Illyria and were changed into serpents is told by Ovid in the *Metamorphoses* IV. 562–602.
Æsculapius, the god of medicine, whose chief seat of worship was at Epidaurus. This legend also is told by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV. 622–744.

the story that Jupiter Ammon — the “Libyan Jove,” so called in allusion to his shrine in the Libyan desert — was the father of Alexander the Great occurs in Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander*. A similar fable represented Jupiter Capitolinus (i.e. of the Capitol) as the father of Scipio Africanus. *Olympias*; the wife of Philip of Macedon.
an allusion to the legend of the sorceress Circe who bewitched men with magic drugs, and then by a touch of her wand transformed them into animals (cf. “herd disguised”) which she kept in subjection.
i.e. either he actually used the serpent’s tongue as an instrument of speech (although “not made” for it, 749), or he caused a voice to sound by impression of the air.
spoke flatteringly. *proem*, introduction; a prelude in music (cf. “tuned”), hence a preface to a poem or speech.
‘as to the latter — “sense,” 554 — I am doubtful whether it was denied to brutes.’ Probably this is an expression of Milton’s own opinion.

of which serpents were supposed to be fond. The snake was thought to refresh its sight in spring-time by rubbing against the fennel-plant. Serpents were supposed to suck the teats of sheep and goats (Newton).
to the extent of giving me the faculty of reason. *inward*; externally there was no change in him (601).
to enjoy what is provided for them. *birth*, produce — ‘what she bears.’
blossoming. *balm*, i.e. the balsam-tree, to which “myrrh,” a kind of thorny shrub, is akin.

an *ignis fatuus*; cf. the German *elf-licht*. M. alludes to the superstition in *L’Allegro*, 104, and *Comus*, 433; but whether he himself believes in it we do not know, as he is careful to add the qualifying words “they say.”
a “Hebraism for the prohibited or forbidden tree” (Newton). *root*, source; used probably with a grim quibble on “Tree.”
a literal rendering of a Hebrew phrase which implies ‘a voice from Heaven.’ *the rest*, for the rest — ‘in all else’ (Lat. *cetera*).

assumes a new character, i.e. feigning indignant sympathy with man. The metaphor is that of ‘playing a part.’ As a young man Milton seems to have been fond of the theatre, which often supplies him with a simile or illustration.
such as Demosthenes; or Isocrates, the “old man eloquent” of his Sonnet “To the Lady Margaret Ley”; or Cicero.
plunged right into the subject (*in medias res*). Probably M. had in mind the abrupt commencement of Cicero’s first Oration against Catiline (Thyer).
The Serpent’s argument is — ‘Your fear of death implies injustice on the part of God: but if He is “not just,” then is He “not God,” and so not to be feared.’

i.e. this perhaps will be the death meant for you, of which you spoke (663). Cf. the New Testament often, e.g. Colossians iii. 9, 10, “ye have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man.”
a variation of Vergil’s *tantaene animis caelestibus irae?* *Aeneid* I. 11.
leaning to, inclined towards (Lat. *inclinabilis*).

The introduction of “signs” and omens after the manner of classical writers occurs at several important points in the action of the poem. Moreover, “all Nature suffered by the guilt of our first parents,” so that these signs are not merely prodigies but appropriate “marks of her sympathising in the fall of man” (Addison).
i.e. that she was eating; an imitation of the Greek use of a participle after verbs of knowledge or perception.
cf. IV. 295–99, 635–38; VIII. 540–75; X. 145–56, 888–98: passages which, taken together, are evidence of Milton’s own conception of the difference between man and woman.
cf. Horace’s *tecum vivere amem, tecum obeam libens*, *Odes* III. 9. 24.
foreboding = Lat. *divinus* in the sense ‘prophetic of.’ *the faltering measure*, the tremulous, uneven ‘beat’ of his heart, excited by the foreboding of evil.

i.e. the pleading expression in her face, showing that she was conscious of guilt, served to introduce the apology she was about to make. The construction seems to be, ‘excuse came as prologue and (came) to lead up to apology’ — *prompt* being a verb.
astonished; cf. Job xvii. 8, “Upright men shall be astonied at this.” *horror chill*; cf. Vergilian expressions like *gelidus tremor* and *frigidus horror*.
the epithet well marks Adam’s distress: even Paradise has suddenly lost its beauty in his eyes and become “wild” and dreary.
in the literal sense ‘deed,’ Lat. *factum*.
cf. Deuteronomy xxxii. 27. For “the Adversary” = Satan, according to the meaning of the name, cf. Job i. 6 (margin), 1 Peter v. 8.
in the sense of Lat. *obligare*, ‘to render liable to punishment, make guilty.’
as Eve was by the Serpent; Adam sinned wilfully. Cf. 1 Timothy ii. 14, “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression.”

it has been remarked that this is the only passage in the poem where M. uses the phrase ‘Original Sin’; the doctrine expressed by it he discusses in the treatise on *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 7 and 11, attributing the first use of the expression to St Augustine.

in this rather far-fetched thought M. is really playing upon the two senses of Lat. *sapere*, ‘to taste’ and ‘to have discernment, be wise’ — both *sapience* (1018) and *savour* (through the French) coming from *sapere*.
cf. the description of Samson’s father Manoah in Judges xiii. 2, “a man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites,” i.e. of the Tribe of Dan.
the worst, greatest; cf. Lat. *extremus*, *ultimus*. *of the first*, i.e. lesser evils, which they may well expect, seeing that they have already experienced the greatest of evils, viz. shame.

the reference is to the banyan-tree or Indian fig. Warton pointed out that M. has followed closely the account of this tree in Gerard’s *Herball*, 1597 (the standard Elizabethan work on botany), where it is called “the arched Indian Fig-tree.”

the description is inaccurate as the leaves of the banyan are small: it is the banana or plantain-tree that has large leaves. Cf. Vergil’s reference to the ‘crescent-shaped shields’ (*lunatae peltae*) of the Amazons, *Aeneid* I. 490.
i.e. as compared with the remote events of which the poem treats; not strictly “of late” in relation to Milton’s own time, because the date of Columbus’s discovery was 1492.
hence Gray’s phrase, “feather-cinctur’d chiefs,” spoken of the Indians of South America, *The Progress of Poesy*, 62.
an allusion to 1 Corinthians xi. 3, “the head of the woman is the man.”

No doubt, an expression of Milton’s own opinion. One of his sneers at Charles I. is that he was influenced so by his wife. Professor Firth has recently noted a curious illustration of Milton’s prejudice against women, viz. his treatment of Boadicea in his *History of Britain*.
